text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNObtain v = HD from a scale factor and distinguish redshift, Hubble time, and cosmic age. 01Multiply galaxy separations by a common factor In the standard large-scale model, the universe is approximately homogeneous and isotropic. For points following the cosmic flow, write their same-time proper separation as D(t) = a(t)χ, using an appropriate fixed comoving separation χ. The dimensionless scale factor a(t) is conventionally one today. Galaxy separations grow by the same factorAn example of galaxy separations increasing uniformly by 1.5, with galaxy sizes held fixed. The grid compares distances; it is not a physical framework or a special centre.View larger diagram ↗ D = aχ, D' = a'χ ⇒ D′D = a′a Primes label values at a different time; they do not denote derivatives here. If a grows from 1 to 1.1, separations of points following the cosmic flow grow by 1.1. This does not make galaxies, solar systems, or atoms expand by the same factor: binding forces determine their internal structures. 02Divide the change by time to obtain Hubble’s law During a short interval Δt, let the scale factor increase by Δa. Since χ stays fixed, ΔD = χΔa = DΔa/a. Divide by Δt to find the rate of separation. ΔDΔt = (ΔaaΔt)D Here a and D are evaluated at the start of the interval. For fixed χ this finite-interval equation is an equality. HΔt ≡ ΔaaΔt, vΔt ≡ ΔDΔt ⇒ vΔt = HΔtD For instantaneous rates the relation is vrec = H(t)D. This is the Hubble–Lemaître relation for uniform expansion. H(t) is a fractional growth rate per unit time; H₀ is its present value. The name “Hubble constant” does not make it constant throughout cosmic history. 03Every observer sees more distant points separate faster Imagine A, B, and C on a line with every gap growing by 1% in a short time. If C is twice as far from A as B is, its separation increases twice as much. From B, both sides follow the same rule. This does not identify Earth as a special centre of expansion. vrec is the change of a same-cosmic-time separation to a distant point. At cosmological distances HD can exceed c without an object locally passing an observer faster than light. The local speed limit and this distant-separation rate are different quantities. 04Stretched wavelengths give cosmological redshift z ≡ λobs−λemitλemit ⇒ 1+z = λobsλemit For emission and observation by comoving observers in a homogeneous, isotropic universe, general relativity supplies the following relation. It is an additional result about light propagating through expanding spacetime, not an algebraic consequence of the definition of z alone. 1+z = anowaemit ⇒ aemit = 11+z (anow=1) At z = 1, the emission-era scale factor was 0.5. At high redshift, inserting z into a special-relativistic Doppler formula is not a general way to infer cosmic distance. Observations can also include peculiar velocities and gravitational redshifts. 05Infer distances in the nearby-universe approximation z ≈ vc, v ≈ H0D ⇒ D ≈ czH0 Use H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ as a round teaching example, not a claim that current measurements have settled on a unique value. One megaparsec is about 3.26 million light-years. At 10 Mpc the example gives 700 km/s; at 100 Mpc, 7,000 km/s. For z = 0.005, v ≈ 1,500 km/s and D ≈ 21.4 Mpc. Peculiar motion can substantially affect nearby-galaxy estimates. At large distances the expansion history and the definition of distance matter, so this approximation is insufficient. 061/H₀ is a timescale, not automatically the age H0 ≈ 70 km/s3.086×1019 km ≈ 2.27×10−18 s−1 tH ≡ 1H0 ≈ 4.41×1017 s ≈ 14 billion years The Hubble time for the example H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Dividing the present separation D by the present recession rate H₀D gives 1/H₀. But that separation need not have grown at its present rate throughout the past. Determining the cosmic age requires the expansion history. Accelerated expansion does not necessarily mean an increasing H: H is a fractional rate, not the absolute rate of growth. Hubble’s law describes the expansion pattern; by itself it does not determine how matter, radiation, and dark energy govern the expansion history. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Lyα has a rest wavelength near 121.6 nm. At z = 3, what wavelength do we observe, and how large was the emission-era scale factor relative to today? Show the answer and reasoning λobs = (1 + 3) × 121.6 = 486.4 nm. With anow = 1, aemit = 1/(1 + 3) = 0.25. This alone does not imply an age one quarter of today’s.
